title: How an extremist network articulated a hoax linking Brazil’s President Lula to child abuse on X

pages.text: Before the 2026 general elections in Brazil, a false story about President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spread quickly. A comment he made about prostate cancer exams was changed to accuse him of child abuse. This happened between September 28 and 29. Aos Fatos, a fact-checking group, looked at 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter). They found that users who support Bolsonaro created and shared this false story.

Some users even used X's AI tool, Grok, to make it seem like Lula was involved in child pornography, using the acronym “CP.” Grok warned that the claim was wordplay and had no proof. However, a short video of Lula's speech was shared, making the false story grow. Influencers and others were asked to make the video go viral. Old, unrelated stories were also used to link Lula to child abuse.

Lula was actually talking about how important it is for men to get prostate exams, comparing it to women's health habits. The false story became very popular, with hashtags like #LULAPEDOPHILE trending. Nikolas Ferreira, a politician who supports Jair Bolsonaro, also shared the altered video. The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) told Nikolas Ferreira to take down his post. They said he changed the meaning of Lula's words.

Even after the original video was clarified, new false stories appeared, trying to connect Lula to a child abuse network. These stories also spread on Telegram and WhatsApp. Some false claims linked Lula to the Marajó archipelago, where child sexual violence is a real problem. However, there is no proof connecting Lula to these crimes. Other posts tried to link Lula to Jeffrey Epstein, using an email that does not prove any conversation happened. Lula's wife and experts said such a call was impossible.

A1-A2.headline: False Story Spreads About Brazil’s Lula

pages.text: Days before Brazil's 2026 general elections on October 4, a statement by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva regarding preventive prostate cancer exams was quickly twisted into a pedophilia accusation against him. A fact-checking investigation by Aos Fatos, published on September 30, 2026, analyzed 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter) to reconstruct how this hoax was spread by Bolsonarista users between September 28 and 29. The manipulation of Lula’s speech began hours before his campaign event in Belém, Pará state, on September 28. Users in the “bolha da resenha” (hangout banter bubble), an ecosystem of mostly anonymous profiles known for extremist political content, experimented with Grok, X’s AI tool.

They forced Grok to generate phrases like “Lula consumes CP,” an acronym for child pornography, by manipulating initial prompts like “cerveja e picanha” (beer and filet steak). Despite Grok’s warnings that the claims were wordplay and lacked supporting records, an edited clip of Lula’s speech, shared widely, gave the false narrative new momentum. Publications called for the video to go viral, urged the mobilization of influencers, and revived old, unrelated episodes to bolster theories associating the president with child abuse. Lula’s original speech focused on the importance of cancer prevention, criticizing men’s reluctance to undergo prostate exams compared to women’s established healthcare culture, including early gynecological exams.

However, the edited quote, such as “Lula saying women ‘learn to be touched ever since they are little’ WHAT THE FUCK, PRESIDENT? Are you NUTS???,” was posted by influencer Pâm at 11.59 p.m. on September 28, and quickly amplified by other accounts, explicitly labeling Lula a “pedophile” by 12.29 a.m. on September 29. The campaign intensified with calls to download and repost the video, suggestions to boost the hashtag #LULAPEDOPHILE, and messages like “it has to go viral.” By 2.48 a.m., a profile proposed mobilizing 10 to 20 influencers.

The narrative gained significant political prominence when Nikolas Ferreira, a prominent Jair Bolsonaro ally and member of the Chamber of Deputies, shared one of the cuts at 9.49 a.m. on September 29, further amplifying the false accusation. Expressions related to this narrative, such as “PROTECT THE CHILDREN” and “LULA DON’T TOUCH THE CHILDREN,” quickly became trending topics on X. The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) subsequently ordered Ferreira to remove his post, stating he had attributed an “entirely different connotation” to Lula’s quote, removing it from its public health context and linking it to crimes.

After going viral, the hoax evolved beyond the Belém speech, with social media accounts introducing new, unrelated episodes and characters to portray Lula as part of an alleged pedophile network. These theories also spread to Telegram and WhatsApp groups, claiming Lula had defended or “trivialized” pedophilia. Some allegations exploited the fact that the speech occurred in Pará, linking it to documented cases of child sexual violence in the Marajó archipelago, despite no evidence connecting Lula to these crimes.

Further posts attempted to associate Lula with Jeffrey Epstein, citing an email attributed to Epstein claiming a phone conversation mediated by Noam Chomsky while Lula was imprisoned. However, the email does not prove the conversation occurred, and Noam Chomsky’s wife denied his mediation. Experts also noted such a call would be incompatible with prison rules. The Federal Prosecution Office (MPF) previously filed a public civil action against Senator Damares Alves for spreading “sensationalist false information” regarding alleged abuses in Marajó Island, which she claimed to have denounced in 2022.

pages.text: In the days leading up to Brazil’s 2026 general elections on October 4, a statement made by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva concerning preventive prostate cancer examinations was rapidly and deliberately distorted into an accusation of pedophilia. An extensive investigation by the fact-checking agency Aos Fatos, originally published on September 30, 2026, meticulously analyzed 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter), detailing the systematic propagation of this hoax by Bolsonarista users across social media platforms between September 28 and 29. The genesis of this narrative manipulation predated Lula’s public statement at a campaign event in Belém, Pará state, on September 28. Users operating within the “bolha da resenha” (hangout banter bubble), an online ecosystem predominantly comprising anonymous profiles characterized by aggressive humor, extremist political content, and the aesthetic replication of chans (anonymous forums known as incubators of the far-right), initiated experiments with Grok, X’s AI assistance tool.

These users intentionally manipulated prompts, such as starting with “cerveja e picanha” (beer and filet steak) and instructing the tool to summarize the expression with its initials, thereby coercing Grok to generate phrases like “Lula consumes CP” — an acronym for child pornography. Despite explicit warnings from the chatbot that such statements constituted wordplay and lacked any factual basis, an edited segment of Lula’s speech, widely disseminated across social media, provided significant impetus to the burgeoning false narrative. Calls for the video’s virality and the mobilization of influencers were prevalent, alongside the reintroduction of historical episodes and figures entirely unconnected to Lula’s original remarks, all aimed at substantiating theories linking the president to child abuse. Lula’s actual discourse at the rally centered on the critical importance of cancer prevention, specifically critiquing men’s resistance to prostate examinations in contrast to women’s established healthcare culture, which, he noted, typically involves gynecological exams from an early age.

However, a truncated quote from his speech, such as ‘Lula saying women ‘learn to be touched ever since they are little’ WHAT THE FUCK, PRESIDENT? Are you NUTS???,’ was first posted at 11.59 p.m. on September 28 by Pâm, an influencer associated with a pro-Bolsonaro content hub. This was swiftly followed by another cut from the same quote by the Space Liberdade account at 12.28 a.m. on September 29, with explicit accusations of Lula being a “pedophile” appearing in subsequent posts by 12.29 a.m. The amplification efforts escalated in the ensuing hours, with users actively encouraging the download and reposting of the video, advocating for the hashtag #LULAPEDOPHILE, and disseminating messages like “it has to go viral.” By 2.48 a.m., a specific profile proposed isolating two sentences from Lula’s speech, creating a dedicated hashtag, and engaging 10 to 20 influencers to promote it. The narrative achieved significant political traction when Nikolas Ferreira, a staunch ally of Jair Bolsonaro and a member of the Chamber of Deputies, published one of the manipulated video clips at 9.49 a.m.

on September 29, further exacerbating the spread of the unsubstantiated accusation. Following Ferreira’s posts, expressions directly associated with this narrative rapidly ascended X’s trending topics. “PROTECT THE CHILDREN,” initially ranked 28th at 9.04 a.m., surged to the top spot by 11.15 a.m. Concurrently, “LULA DON’T TOUCH THE CHILDREN” occupied fourth place, and “pedophile” was 20th. On September 30, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) issued a 24-hour ultimatum to Nikolas Ferreira to remove his post, with Minister Estela Aranha asserting that he had ascribed an “entirely different connotation” to the original quote, divorcing it from its public health context and illicitly associating it with criminal behavior. Once the hoax achieved viral status, its reliance on the specifics of the Belém speech diminished. Social media accounts began to resurrect unrelated episodes and characters to frame Lula as a participant in an alleged pedophile network or ring.

These conspiratorial theories permeated Telegram and WhatsApp groups monitored by Aos Fatos, evolving from claims that Lula had merely defended or “trivialized” pedophilia to assertions of a “likely inclination to pedophilia,” citing isolated incidents as purported evidence. One particularly egregious allegation exploited the geographical context of Lula’s speech in Pará state, attempting to link him to documented cases of sexual violence against children in the local Marajó archipelago. Despite the reality of child sexual violence in the region, there is no verifiable evidence connecting Lula to such crimes. Furthermore, some posts incorporated statements made in 2022 by Senator Damares Alves, then a minister in Bolsonaro’s cabinet, who claimed to have been attacked for denouncing abuses on Marajó Island. These allegations, however, were not substantiated by investigative bodies, and the Federal Prosecution Office (MPF) subsequently initiated a public civil action against Alves for disseminating what they characterized as “sensationalist false information involving sexual abuse and torture to the children of Marajó.”

Additional posts sought to establish an association between Lula and Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced US financier. The purported evidence for this connection was an email attributed to Epstein, in which he claimed to have conversed with Lula by phone, mediated by Noam Chomsky, during Lula’s imprisonment in Curitiba, Brazil. While the email’s existence is confirmed, it provides no conclusive proof that such a conversation ever transpired. Valeria Chomsky, Noam’s wife, explicitly denied his mediation, and the Social Communications Office of the Presidency, upon the email’s initial public disclosure, stated that “the referred phone call never happened.” Experts interviewed by Folha de S. Paulo newspaper further corroborated that such a phone call would have been incompatible with the regulations of the Federal Police prison ward where Lula was incarcerated. It is also noteworthy that other Brazilian politicians, including former president Jair Bolsonaro, were mentioned by Epstein, whom the financier once referred to as “the man.”

title: Peru’s Indigenous people in Cutivireni and Oviri take the front line against Amazon wildfires

pages.text: Wildfires are a big problem around the world in 2026, made worse by hot, dry weather. In places like France, many people have had to leave their homes. The United Nations says that a strong El Niño will make things even hotter, like in 2024 when there were many fires in the Amazon.

Indigenous people in Peru’s Amazon rainforest are now working to stop these fires. Communities in Cutivireni and Oviri asked Cool Earth for help. They wanted to learn how to fight fires. Cool Earth already worked with other Indigenous groups, so it was easy to set up four fire teams. One team, the Chullachaqui fire crew in Cutivireni, has already put out several fires.

They learned to watch for satellite fire alerts and use a flag system to know when it's safe to use fire for traditional practices. They also got training to stop small fires from becoming big problems. This helps protect their homes and the rainforest, which is important for fighting climate change.

One fire in August was very big, burning for four days and destroying 50 hectares of land. Cool Earth wants to give more training and money to Indigenous people so they can fight more fires in the Amazon. Chullachaqui (Chullachaqui): Tên một linh hồn rừng Amazon. pages.text: The year 2026 has been marked by widespread wildfires globally, intensified by the heat and dryness associated with the climate crisis. Events such as those near Bordeaux, France, have displaced 200,000 people and caused fatalities in Spain. Smoke from fires has also impacted cities across the Canada-U.S. border. The United Nations warns that a severe El Niño phenomenon is expected to exacerbate these conditions as seasons change in the Southern Hemisphere, potentially leading to wildfires similar to the worst Amazonian fires in two decades, which occurred in 2024.

In response to increasing fire and drought risks, Indigenous communities in the Peruvian Amazon are taking proactive measures. Communities in Cutivireni and Oviri partnered with Cool Earth to enhance their fire-fighting capabilities. Leveraging an established relationship and previous work with the Central Asháninka of the Ene River on the Paamari programme, Cool Earth facilitated the creation of four fire crews.

The newly formed Chullachaqui fire crew in Cutivireni, named after an Amazonian forest spirit, has already successfully managed multiple blazes. Their training, derived from the Paamari programme, focuses on three core concepts: monitoring satellite fire weather alerts, implementing a flag-based system for safe traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small fires. This approach helps prevent minor incidents from escalating into widespread devastation for Indigenous populations and the rainforest.

Julio Acosta, Cool Earth’s Forest Data Manager, commended the communities for effectively applying their training. An early test in August saw community brigade members from Tsyapo and Pajonal, alerted by local residents, join forces with partners in Central Cutivireni to extinguish a fire, demonstrating the effectiveness of their workshops. These brigades prioritize prevention, using measures like the flag system to reduce fire occurrences, which Acosta notes is often less visible but crucial.

Beyond protecting their homes, these Indigenous communities serve as vital custodians of the rainforest, a critical global asset in combating the climate crisis. Rainforests contribute 23 percent of the climate mitigation needed to stabilize global temperatures. Their destruction by wildfires not only depletes natural carbon stores but also releases significant amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

While many fires are contained, a severe August fire in Cutivireni, rated three out of five on Peru’s national disaster response scale, raged for four days, destroying 50 hectares of land. Cool Earth aims to expand training and financial support to meet the growing demand for wildfire management in the Peruvian Amazon. Chullachaqui (Chullachaqui): Tên một linh hồn rừng Amazon. pages.text: The year 2026 has been characterized by an alarming proliferation of wildfires across the globe, a phenomenon significantly exacerbated by the escalating heat and aridity driven by the climate crisis. Notable incidents include outbreaks on the periphery of Bordeaux, France, which necessitated the evacuation of 200,000 individuals and resulted in fatalities in Spain. Furthermore, smoke plumes have traversed the Canada-U.S. border, enveloping major urban centers in smog. Projections indicate a continuation of these fire risks as the Southern Hemisphere transitions seasons, with a severe El Niño phenomenon, as warned by the United Nations, poised to intensify pressure on an already scorching planet. This could precipitate conditions akin to those in 2024, which witnessed the most devastating Amazonian wildfires in two decades.

In anticipation of heightened fire and drought risks in the forthcoming months, Indigenous communities within the Amazon rainforest are proactively assuming critical roles as fire brigade members. This initiative not only safeguards their ancestral homes but also preserves a vital natural resource integral to global climate change mitigation efforts. Prior to this year’s El Niño weather pattern, Indigenous populations from Peru’s Cutivireni and Oviri communities engaged with Cool Earth, seeking to bolster their preparedness for the impending fire season. The organization’s long-established rapport with these two Indigenous groups, coupled with its experience collaborating with the Central Asháninka of the Ene River to develop the Paamari programme, facilitated the swift establishment of four fire crews across communities already demonstrating a readiness for action.

In Cutivireni, the recently constituted Chullachaqui fire crew, named after an Amazonian forest spirit, has already successfully confronted multiple blazes. This crew comprehends the indispensable role they play in safeguarding their land, residences, and livelihoods. An initial test of their training occurred in early August: alerted by residents in the Tsyapo and Pajonal communities, brigade members converged with their counterparts in Central Cutivireni to suppress the fire, an endeavor they successfully accomplished. Julio Acosta, Cool Earth’s Forest Data Manager, expressed profound admiration for the communities’ adept utilization of the resources and training provided, noting that “This early action taken in Tsyapo and Pajonal demonstrates how effectively they put into practice what they’ve learned in the workshops.”

The training methodology was directly adapted from the foundational concepts of the Paamari programme. The Cool Earth initiative with Cutivireni and Oviri is structured around three core tenets: enhanced monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the implementation of a flag-based system to delineate safe periods for traditional fire practices, and comprehensive practical training designed to contain nascent blazes and avert their potential to inflict widespread devastation upon Indigenous communities and the rainforest. The communities themselves frequently serve as the brigades’ primary reconnaissance, providing early alerts regarding smoke or flames. Operating in close coordination with local authorities, brigade members initially assess wildfires and endeavor to control them in their incipient stages, thereby precluding the necessity for more complex interventions by governmental authorities.

Acosta underscored the paramount importance of prevention over initial response, stating, “This tends to be less visible,” but emphasizing that measures such as the flag system significantly reduce fire occurrences. He added that the “initiative and eagerness to learn more from the brigade members motivates us to expand and improve the work we’ve been implementing together.” Beyond the immediate protection of their homes, these Indigenous communities function as crucial custodians of the rainforest, a globally significant asset in the battle against the climate crisis. According to the World Resources Institute, rainforests contribute 23 percent of the climate mitigation required to stabilize global temperatures; their destruction by wildfires not only depletes the world’s natural carbon stores but also releases substantial quantities of carbon back into the atmosphere.

While many fires are effectively managed, an August fire in Cutivireni, which registered a score of three out of five on Peru’s national disaster response scale, raged for four days, ultimately destroying 50 hectares of land, an area roughly equivalent to 70 football pitches. Eyewitnesses reported that “little that’s left or [that] survived.” In light of the increasing strain on these communities, Cool Earth aspires to establish further training programs, transforming the current initiative into a fully fledged project. By providing Indigenous people with enhanced financial resources and training capabilities, the organization aims to address the ever-growing demand for wildfire management expertise within the Peruvian Amazon.
